units.title: Arbitrum Nitro and Orbit chains
angles: Arithmetic and control flow. Read the interpreter this network runs at the release its endpoint reports, and any compiler, bytecode rewriting, caching or code analysis stage in front of it. Cover the 256 bit integer library and its pinned version, MULMOD, ADDMOD, DIV, SDIV, MOD, SMOD, SIGNEXTEND, SAR, SHL, SHR, BYTE, EXP, the comparisons, JUMP and JUMPI with the jump destination analysis, KECCAK256, MCOPY, memory expansion and CALLDATALOAD. Compare each with the Ethereum specification at the edges that OPCODES.md lists, and read the release notes and fix commits since the versions OPCODES.md records. Then rerun the scripts in research/network-risk/tools/opdiff (battery.py, targeted.py, pmdiff.py, pmdiff2.py, swaps.py, replay.py) for this unit's chain ids, write the outputs into your work directory, and add vectors for anything the reading makes suspicious. Report every result that differs from the specification, every release that changed these paths, how a wrong result would change the pool math in src/libraries (TickMath, BitMath, FullMath, SqrtPriceMath, SwapMath, TickBitmap) or the logic that depends on it, and which validators could run a different code path than the public endpoint.

Known weaknesses. Collect security advisories, audit reports, bug bounty write-ups, incident post-mortems and open issues for this network's execution client, precompiles and system contracts from the last two years, including behaviour the network calls by design. For each, decide whether an ordinary account could use it against funds in the PoolManager.

code.task: The build of this checkout is in research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json (runtime 24,009 bytes), research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pyevm.py is a reference EVM in Python, and research/network-risk/OPCODES.md holds what is already tested and read, with a section on what cycle 10 added and a list of what is not covered. Leads L-623 and L-624. On Monad (chain id 143, RPC https://rpc.monad.xyz, PoolManager 0x188d586ddcf52439676ca21a244753fa19f9ea8e) block execution runs a frequently called contract as native x86 code that the client's compiler emits, and simulated calls on the RPC always use the interpreter. Cycle 10 transcribed the compiled multiplication paths (cycles/010/theme-monad-compiled-mul.work holds the transcription harness and a copy list of the v0.16.5 source; a source copy is in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-v4-core/0b315df9-4a6b-5032-a881-24bad3c79fc5/scratchpad/opsrc-monad/v0165/ if it still exists, otherwise fetch from raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/v0.16.5/<path>). The compiled code that decides settlement is still unread and untested. Part one: read and transcribe, at the level of emitted instructions and runtime helpers, the v0.16.5 code generation for RETURNDATASIZE, RETURNDATACOPY (with its bounds check), CALLVALUE, CALLER, TLOAD, TSTORE, the KECCAK256 runtime helper, CALLDATALOAD, CALLDATACOPY, MCOPY, and SIGNEXTEND with a variable index, at each operand location the emitter distinguishes (stack slot, AVX register, general register, literal). Run the transcriptions on the exact instruction sequences of Currency.transfer (src/types/Currency.sol), balanceOfSelf, CurrencyDelta.applyDelta (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol), CurrencyReserves and _settle (src/PoolManager.sol) as they appear in the built runtime, and compare with pyevm.py. Also read how the compiled CALL and STATICCALL return into the caller: what happens to the return data buffer, the transient storage journal and the memory of the caller when the callee reverts, and whether a revert inside compiled code rolls back TSTORE through the same journal as the interpreter. Part two: find out whether debug_traceTransaction on Monad (callTracer with withLog works on the public endpoint) re-executes the transaction in the interpreter or returns frames recorded at block execution; the source of the RPC and trace path answers this. If it re-executes, adapt cycles/010/theme-megaeth-executor.work/frames.py to Monad and compare receipt status and logs with the trace for mined PoolManager transactions that call sync, settle, settleFor, take, mint or burn, and for transactions with a reverted frame that entered unlock followed by a completed unlock. If it does not, compare receipts with eth_call at the parent block for transactions at index 0 of their block. Report how many transactions of each kind were compared, and say plainly which settlement instructions now have compiled-path evidence and which still have none. A compiled fault here would credit a payer who did not pay, so treat any mismatch as a finding and any path left unread as a lead.

The build of this checkout is in research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json (runtime 24,009 bytes), research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pyevm.py is a reference EVM in Python, and research/network-risk/OPCODES.md holds what is already tested and read, with a section on what cycle 10 added and a list of what is not covered. Lead L-625. Every mined check so far uses Swap events. ModifyLiquidity events (topic0 = keccak of ModifyLiquidity(bytes32,address,int24,int24,int256,bytes32)) carry no amounts, so the amounts block production paid to liquidity providers who removed liquidity or collected fees have never been checked on any network. On Monad (143) blocks run compiled code, on MegaETH (4326) a closed compiling executor, on HyperEVM (999) a closed validator, and Tempo (4217) and Arc (5042) have one client each; simulated calls reach none of the first three. For each of these five networks (endpoints and PoolManager addresses in research/network-risk/state/networks.json; research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/swaps.py and replay.py show how logs and extsload are read, including the alternative log endpoints), collect mined ModifyLiquidity events with negative liquidityDelta and with zero liquidityDelta. For each, compute what the source says the PoolManager owed: principal from SqrtPriceMath.getAmount0Delta and getAmount1Delta at the pool's slot0 before the call (src/libraries/Pool.sol modifyLiquidity, src/libraries/SqrtPriceMath.sol; tools/opdiff/v4math.py has amount0_delta and amount1_delta), and fees from Position.update (src/libraries/Position.sol: FullMath.mulDiv(feeGrowthInside - feeGrowthInsideLast, liquidity, 2^128)) using the position's feeGrowthInsideLast and the tick feeGrowthOutside values read with extsload at the parent block (StateLibrary slot layout: _pools at slot 6; position key is keccak of owner, tickLower, tickUpper, salt). Then reconstruct what was really paid in the same transaction: ERC-20 Transfer events from the PoolManager, native value in call frames from debug_traceTransaction where it exists, ERC-6909 Transfer events, or balance differences by eth_getBalance and balanceOf between the parent block and the block for single-action transactions. Keep to transactions whose only PoolManager action for that currency is the removal, so the amounts can be attributed, and say how many were set aside. Report per network how many removals and fee collections matched to the unit, how many differed and by how much, and whether any difference exceeds the rounding the source allows (one unit per amount, in the pool's favour). If historical state is pruned on an endpoint, use the newest events and say so. A removal that paid more than the source formula is a finding; a network where nothing could be checked is a lead.

The build of this checkout is in research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json (runtime 24,009 bytes), research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pyevm.py is a reference EVM in Python, and research/network-risk/OPCODES.md holds what is already tested and read, with a section on what cycle 10 added and a list of what is not covered. Leads L-626, L-627, L-629 and L-547. On three networks the code that produces blocks is not the code that answers eth_call: MegaETH (4326, closed compiling executor on the sequencer, RPC replicas apply its results), HyperEVM (999, closed validator hl-node, public archive clients nanoreth and hyper-evm-sync), and Polygon (137, bor block producers run BlockSTM parallel execution, RPC executes serially). cycles/010/theme-megaeth-executor.work/frames.py compares the receipt of a mined transaction with a second execution by debug_traceTransaction and classifies frames; reuse it. Part one, MegaETH: without building any software, extend the cycle 10 evidence to the cases it did not contain. Search mined PoolManager transactions (0xacb7e78fa05d562e0a5d3089ec896d57d057d38e) for sync, settle, settleFor, take, mint, burn or clear inside a frame that reverted while the transaction went on, and for liquidity removals and fee collections; compare receipt status, logs and, where the endpoint allows it, the post-state of the touched storage slots (eth_getStorageAt at the block against prestateTracer in diff mode) with the second execution. Also read the stateless validator's documentation: does any public party run it and publish mismatches. Part two, HyperEVM: read the source of nanoreth (hl-archive-node/nanoreth) and hyper-evm-sync (hyperliquid-dex/hyper-evm-sync) on raw.githubusercontent.com and answer whether either computes the state root and receipts root of each block and compares them with what hl-node produced, and whether it stops on a mismatch; cite file and line. Then find mined HyperEVM PoolManager transactions with a reverted frame that entered unlock followed by a completed unlock, and with settle or take in a reverted frame, and compare the validator's receipt with the archive client's debug_traceTransaction (public nanoreth endpoints are listed in tools/opdiff/swaps.py and earlier work directories). Part three, Polygon: apply frames.py to mined Polygon PoolManager transactions (0x67366782805870060151383f4bbff9dab53e5cd6) with a reverted unlock frame followed by a completed unlock and to transactions that call sync and settle, and compare receipt with re-execution. Read in bor v2.11.1 whether transient storage and the access list are per transaction under BlockSTM (core/blockstm, core/state) and whether a re-executed incarnation starts from a clean transient map. Report counts per network and per kind, and say plainly which rollback cases now have mined evidence and which have none. A receipt that differs from re-execution is a finding.

The build of this checkout is in research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json (runtime 24,009 bytes), research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pyevm.py is a reference EVM in Python, and research/network-risk/OPCODES.md holds what is already tested and read, with a section on what cycle 10 added and a list of what is not covered. Leads L-628 and L-633. Cycle 10 found that Tempo and Arc route the KECCAK256 opcode through a process-wide cache in alloy-primitives (feature keccak-cache-global, crate fixed-cache), which sits in front of every hash of 1 to 87 bytes. That covers every mapping slot (balanceOf, allowance, isOperator, _pools, positions, ticks) and every transient delta slot of the PoolManager, so a wrong cached result would place a balance or a delta at another slot. It was read for Tempo and Arc only (cycles/010/stablecoin-l1.research.json and its verdicts hold the reading for fixed-cache 0.1.10 and 0.1.8). Part one: for reth v2.11.0 (Ethereum), op-reth v2.9.0-rc.1 and v2.8.1 (ethereum-optimism/optimism rust/), base v1.5.6, world-chain v2.8.2, conduit-op-reth v2.5.1 (if public), xlayer-reth v0.0.7, celo-reth v2.2.0 and the MegaETH stateless validator, read the binary crate's Cargo.toml and the Cargo.lock at the tag and say whether keccak-cache-global is enabled, through which dependency edge, and with which alloy-primitives and fixed-cache versions and features. For each version that differs from the two already read, reread the get and insert paths: key equality (length and every byte), the lock or seqlock protocol, the epoch feature, and what a reader sees while a writer is in the middle of an insert. Say whether revm's KECCAK256 instruction and the storage key hashing of the state provider both go through the cache. Part two: test it. With tools/opdiff/battery.py as a pattern, send KECCAK256 of inputs of length 1 to 88 bytes that collide in the cache's index bits (derive the index function from the source: which hash, which bits) to each of those networks' endpoints (state/networks.json), interleaved so that one bucket is evicted and refilled, many times and in parallel batches, and compare every result with the Python keccak in tools/opdiff/evm.py. Include the exact preimage shapes the PoolManager hashes: 64 bytes (mapping slots, delta slots: address then currency) and 85 or so bytes for position keys. Part three, L-633: X Layer pins ruint 1.18.0 and Base 1.19.0, inside advisory RUSTSEC-2026-0220. In the revm-interpreter versions they pin, does every SHL, SHR, SAR and BYTE handler clamp the amount before calling ruint, and does any precompile or handler of xlayer-reth or base call a wrapping, overflowing or checked shift with an unclamped amount. Report any wrong hash as a finding and any client whose configuration could not be read as a lead.
